findings.title: Completing one work order returned a still-faulty device to clinical service, across any tenant, any number of times
findings.description:
BiomedicalService.complete_work_order carried three defects on a LIVE, migration-backed table (biomed_work_orders) reachable at POST /biomedical/work-orders/{wo_id}/complete.

(1) The lookup was filter_by(id=wo_id) with no tenant predicate, and the service had no tenant context at all to scope it with. A caller acting for lab A completed lab B's work order and flipped lab B's device to available. The router requires system:admin, but admin is a lab-scoped role here — only master_admin and ministry_admin are cross-tenant — so this was a genuine cross-tenant mutation, not an intended override.

(2) Closing ANY work order set device.status = AVAILABLE unconditionally. A class III ventilator held out_of_service with two open work orders became available when only the first was completed; the second fault was never touched. Returning a device to clinical service is a safety decision, and closing one ticket says nothing about the faults the other tickets were raised for.

(3) No row lock and no terminal-state guard: two concurrent transactions both committed the same terminal transition, the later write silently replaced the earlier one's cost and action record, and `version` never moved off 1 although the model carries the optimistic-lock column.

findings.title: 28 mutating service methods select a row by id with no tenant predicate anywhere in the method
findings.description:
The defect fixed in NR-016 is an instance of a pattern, not a one-off. An AST pass over backend/app found 28 mutating methods (they set .status, commit, or delete) whose row lookup is filter_by(id=...) and which contain no lab_id or tenant reference anywhere in the method body.

By domain: blood_bank 5, critical_care 4, lifecycle_platform 4, national/notification_platform 4, biomedical 3, command_center 2, document_intelligence 2, ems 2, pilot_platform 1, public_health 1.

A second pass split them by whether the method name is called from any api/routes module: 24 apparently route-reachable, 4 not.

CAVEAT, stated because it changes what this number means. The reachability test matches on method NAME, so generic names over-count: the four notification_platform save()/delete() hits and the two document_intelligence delete()/unregister() hits are very likely matching an unrelated class. Treat 24 as an upper bound, not a count of confirmed live holes. Only NR-016 was individually traced end to end and reproduced.

THE 4 NOT ROUTE-REACHABLE ARE INFORMATIVE. blood_bank start_transfusion() and complete_transfusion() are tenant-blind but SUPERSEDED: the routes call start_transfusion_safely() and complete_transfusion_safely(transfusion_id, lab_id, body), which do take the tenant. So the earlier blood-bank hardening left the unscoped originals in place rather than removing them. They are dead weight that reads like a live hole and would become one if anything called them again.

TRACED 2026-09-25, and the heuristic's over-count is now demonstrated twice:
  critical_care.discharge_patient() — SAFE / DEAD-SUPERSEDED. The route calls discharge_patient_safely(admission_id, body, lab_id), which has the lab filter, .with_for_update(), is_deleted, a terminal-state guard over {discharged, transferred, deceased}, required-field validation, version += 1 and a bed lock with an ownership check — wrapped by ClinicalCommandGuard with If-Match and an idempotency key. findings.title: HospitalService._get_entity compiled to WHERE false, so ten hospital routes answered 404 for records that exist
findings.description: The helper filtered with Python's 'not' instead of SQLAlchemy's '~': db.query(model).filter(model.id == entity_id, model.lab_id == lab_id, not model.is_deleted). model.is_deleted is an InstrumentedAttribute with no __bool__ override, so bool(...) is default object truthiness (True) and 'not model.is_deleted' is the literal False. SQLAlchemy folds a AND b AND false to false, so the compiled statement was 'WHERE false' — the id and tenant predicates did not fail to match, they were eliminated. The helper never returned a row and always raised NotFoundError. All ten route call sites in app/routes/hospital.py were affected, including assign_bed, discharge_bed, transfer_bed, update_department, and complete_surgical_safety_checklist.

findings.description: An InstrumentedAttribute does not override __bool__, so 'not Model.attr' is the literal False. SQLAlchemy accepts it into the WHERE clause and folds the conjunction (a AND b AND false is false), compiling to 'WHERE false' and ELIMINATING every other predicate in the same call, lab_id included. An AST sweep found 28 such predicates: 20 in app/lims/routes.py (Department, Instrument, InstrumentModel, Manufacturer, Specimen, Order, Panel, Result, QCProgram, Reagent, Consumable, Lot, Supplier, Storage, ReferenceRangeDef, DeltaCheckRule, AutoValidationRule, LabReport), 3 in app/pharmacy/inventory.py and services.py (batch selection excluded every batch rather than only quarantined ones), 1 in app/pharmacy/routes.py (_get_or_404 could never find a row), 3 in app/radiology/pacs.py (an image share could not be resolved or revoked) and 1 in app/routes/admin.py (the lab-approval queue was permanently empty, so no registered lab could be activated).

findings.root_cause: A present control was not applied. _authenticate_client() already existed in app/routes/oauth2.py and /oauth2/token had always called it; introspect and revoke simply omitted the call. Neither endpoint scoped its token lookup to the calling client either.
findings.evidence: Negative proof on real PostgreSQL with the control surgically removed and everything else left fixed: unauthenticated POST /oauth2/introspect returned 200 {"active":true,"client_id":"cid-...","user_id":111,"scope":"openid",...}; unauthenticated POST /oauth2/revoke returned 200 {"message":"Token revoked"}; and client A, authenticated correctly, introspected client B's token and received B's user_id 222. The two legitimate-caller tests passed throughout, so the suite is not merely asserting 401.
findings.affected_users: Every OAuth2/OIDC client and every user holding a token issued through it.
findings.security_impact: RFC 7662 §2.1 requires authorization on the introspection endpoint explicitly 'to prevent token scanning attacks'. Without it the endpoint is an oracle for whether an arbitrary token is valid, and a hit identifies the user behind it. Unauthenticated revocation is a targeted denial of service against any live session or grant.
findings.operational_impact: Any session or grant could be terminated by an unauthenticated caller who learned its token value.
findings.recommended_fix: Applied: authenticate the client on both endpoints and scope every token lookup to that client. REMAINING RESIDUAL: _authenticate_client accepts a public client (token_endpoint_auth_method='none') on client_id alone. For revocation that is standards-conformant (RFC 7009 §2.1 via RFC 6749 §2.3), but for introspection it means a caller holding a token plus a public client_id can still introspect that client's tokens. Tightening it is a policy decision about who may introspect — resource servers rather than public clients — and was deliberately not invented here.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED. client_id/client_secret added to OAuth2IntrospectRequest and OAuth2RevokeRequest; both handlers call _authenticate_client and raise 401 on failure; both token queries carry OAuth2Token.client_id == client.client_id. Introspection answers active=false rather than an error for another client's token (RFC 7662), and revocation answers 200 regardless (RFC 7009 §2.2), so neither becomes an oracle.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/verification/test_oauth2_client_authentication.py, 7 tests against real PostgreSQL.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Unauthenticated introspect and revoke return 401; a wrong secret returns 401; an authenticated client can still introspect and revoke its own token; a client cannot read or revoke another client's token, proven for revocation by reading is_revoked back with SQL.
findings.regression_risk: A deployed client that called introspect or revoke without credentials now receives 401. That is the intended change; such a client was relying on the defect.
findings.evidence_strength: VERIFIED

findings.root_cause: ORM declarations disagreed with the migration that built the table, and SQLAlchemy does not coerce an integer literal on a Boolean-typed column — it binds the integer and PostgreSQL rejects it. No test caught this because the suites covering these routes build their tables from the ORM with create_all(), where Integer and Boolean both yield a usable column and the drift cannot exist.
findings.evidence: Measured on gula_canon (built by migrations to head 20260909_0001). Before the fix, POST /oauth2/token — code untouched by any change in this unit — returned 500 with 'operator does not exist: boolean = integer' on 'oauth2_clients.is_active = 1'. After the fix the same request returned 200 with a real access token. A sweep across all 18 declarative bases, comparing 407 of 423 physical tables, found exactly 4 boolean/non-boolean mismatches and 0 after the fix.
findings.affected_users: Every consumer of the OAuth2/OIDC provider: /token, /introspect, /revoke, /authorize.
findings.security_impact: The provider could not authenticate a client at all, so no OAuth2 flow could complete. The direction of failure was closed, not open: requests 500'd rather than succeeding unauthorized.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None observed. The failure aborted the transaction before any write.
findings.operational_impact: OAuth2/OIDC was advertised in the route table and in the OIDC discovery document while being wholly unusable.
findings.intersections: Same create_all() blindness recorded under TEST-001: a suite that builds tables from the ORM cannot observe ORM/migration drift. This is a further class of defect that blindness has hidden.
findings.recommended_fix: Applied. The migration is canonical and immutable, so the ORM and the route literals were corrected to match it, not the reverse.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED. Four columns changed from Integer to Boolean across three model files, and the 12 integer literal sites in app/routes/oauth2.py changed to .is_(True)/.is_(False)/True/False. ATTRIBUTION, measured rather than assumed: the load-bearing repair is the route literals — 'IS true' is valid SQL against a boolean column whatever the ORM declares — so reverting only the model types leaves the OAuth2 tests passing while the drift guard fails. The model corrections are therefore defence-in-depth that removes the trap, not what restored the provider.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/verification/test_boolean_column_drift.py (3 tests, all 18 bases, 407 tables) plus the restored /oauth2/token 200. Both guards require real PostgreSQL and skip rather than pass without it.
findings.acceptance_criteria: No ORM column disagrees with the database about being a boolean, across every declarative base; the guard proves it compared >350 tables so it cannot pass by measuring nothing; every base imports.
findings.regression_risk: service_accounts.is_active was a latent trap rather than a live failure — its callers already used .is_(True)/= False — so correcting its type changes no behaviour. The OAuth2 sites were already 500ing.
findings.evidence_strength: VERIFIED
findings.status: FIXED
findings.title: The entire OAuth2/OIDC provider was non-functional on PostgreSQL: boolean columns compared against integers
findings.description: Migration 20260716_0015 created oauth2_clients.is_active, oauth2_clients.is_confidential, oauth2_tokens.is_revoked and service_accounts.is_active as sa.Boolean(). All four ORM models declared them Integer, and app/routes/oauth2.py compared and assigned integer literals (is_active == 1, is_revoked == 0, is_revoked = 1, is_revoked=0). PostgreSQL rejects this outright: 'operator does not exist: boolean = integer'. Every affected endpoint returned 500.

findings.root_cause: Not a type mismatch but two independent designs under one name. ORM: drug_code (String), indication_code, age_min_months/age_max_months (Integer), lab_id, metadata, pregnancy_note, breastfeeding_note, fhir_id, fhir_resource_type. Physical: drug_id (Integer), indication (varchar 300), age_min_years/age_max_years (double), duration, evidence_level, geriatric_note, pregnancy_category, source, is_active, sync_id.
findings.evidence: Measured on gula_canon: ORM declares 29 columns, the table has 30, only 19 names overlap. A bare ORM read raises (psycopg2.errors.UndefinedColumn) column pharmacy_dose_guidelines.drug_code does not exist. Both served routes confirmed returning 500 through the verification harness as an authenticated pharmacist.
findings.affected_users: Anyone using the pharmacy dose calculator or renal adjustment endpoints.
findings.clinical_impact: The dose calculation capability is advertised and wholly non-functional. It fails closed — no incorrect dose is returned — but a clinician gets a 500 where the platform claims to offer dosing support.
findings.data_integrity_impact: The physical table has no lab_id column at all, while the ORM extends TenantAuditEntity and expects one. Tenant isolation for dose guidelines is therefore structurally impossible in the current physical design, independently of the read failure.

findings.recommended_fix: HUMAN DECISION REQUIRED — deliberately not resolved autonomously. Three questions must be answered before any code moves: (1) is a dose guideline keyed by drug_code (a string) or drug_id (a foreign key)? (2) are the age bounds expressed in MONTHS or YEARS? These are different clinical quantities and mapping one onto the other because both are numeric is exactly the error the engineering mission forbids. (3) must dose guidelines be tenant-scoped, given the physical table has no lab_id — are they reference data shared platform-wide, or per-lab? Only once these are settled can the ORM, a migration, or both be reconciled.

findings.acceptance_criteria: ORM columns and physical columns agree; both dose routes return 200; tenancy behaviour matches the recorded decision.

findings.data_integrity_impact: Cross-generation foreign keys cannot resolve. The concrete instance is recorded as NR-063: pharmacy_sale_lines.drug_catalog_id is character varying and references an integer primary key, so PostgreSQL could not create the constraint and the relationship is unenforced.
findings.operational_impact: Every query naming one of the 144 columns raises rather than returning a wrong answer. Reachability per endpoint was NOT measured; only the pharmacy dose routes (NR-056) are confirmed live-failing.
findings.intersections: Root cause of NR-057's 144 String-vs-INTEGER columns. Parent of NR-063. NR-056 is the pharmacy_dose_guidelines instance. CLAUDE.md gates app/financial/, whose fin_* Integer-vs-UUID columns are the same class in a fourth flavour.
findings.contradictions: Prior task history records 'rewrite the 17 Generation-B pharmacy ORM models from the physical schema' as completed, yet 62 pharmacy columns still disagree with the physical schema on type. Recorded as a tension rather than resolved: the rewrite may have covered fields without covering the inherited primary key, which comes from base.py and not from the model modules. Not verified either way here.
findings.recommended_fix: HUMAN DECISION REQUIRED, deliberately not taken. Two coherent directions, and they are not equivalent in cost: (A) migrate the 70 integer-keyed tables to varchar ULID primary keys, which is a data migration touching every foreign key that references them; or (B) revert the eight base classes to integer sequence keys and migrate the 11 varchar tables, which discards the ULID model the newer migrations were written for. A third option — accept the split permanently and make the boundary explicit — is viable only if the cross-generation foreign keys of NR-063 are resolved. Whichever is chosen must be one decision applied consistently; the present state is the cost of not having made it.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: NOT APPLIED and not attempted. What IS applied is containment: the NR-057 pin (test_hard_error_type_drift.py) blocks growth, so the problem cannot get larger while the decision is pending. No base class, model or migration was altered.
findings.verification_method: Once decided: every mapped id and *_id column agrees with its physical column, and the NR-057 pin shrinks to zero.
findings.acceptance_criteria: One identity model per domain, implemented consistently in both the ORM and the physical schema, with every cross-table reference resolvable.
findings.regression_risk: Changing a primary key type is a data migration with platform-wide FK consequences, not an annotation change. Doing it per-table rather than per-decision would deepen the split.

findings.title: Two identity generations coexist in one database: eight ORM bases declare ULID string keys, 70 tables use integer sequences — HUMAN DECISION
findings.description: Eight domain base classes — pharmacy, nursing, radiology, nhdw, clinical, ehr, national and care_continuum — each declare `id = Column(String(26), primary_key=True, default=_ulid)`. The migrated database implements that for 11 tables and uses integer sequences for 70. The pharmacy domain straddles the line inside itself: 4 tables carry varchar ids and 23 carry integer.

findings.root_cause: A direct consequence of the two identity generations recorded as NR-062: a ULID-keyed table referencing an integer-keyed table.
findings.evidence: Read from information_schema on gula_canon. pharmacy_sale_lines carries exactly two foreign-key constraints — pharmacy_sale_lines_lab_id_fkey to labs, and pharmacy_sale_lines_sale_id_fkey to pharmacy_sales. There is no constraint on drug_catalog_id. By contrast pharmacy_drug_substitution_rules, also a varchar-id table, declares its original_drug_catalog_id and alternative_drug_catalog_id as integer and so matches the catalogue correctly — the same domain is inconsistent with itself about this.
findings.affected_users: Any laboratory or pharmacy using point-of-sale dispensing.
findings.clinical_impact: Dispensing traceability. Not asserted beyond that: whether this breaks a specific recall or audit workflow was not traced, and is not claimed here.
findings.data_integrity_impact: A sale line is the record of which drug was sold. That reference is neither enforced by the database nor resolvable by a join, so sales cannot be reliably attributed to a catalogue entry. Whether any such orphaned rows exist in a production deployment was NOT measured — gula_canon is a freshly migrated schema with no sales data.
findings.intersections: Child of NR-062. The 87 pharmacy foreign-key constraints were counted but NOT individually audited for this pattern — other instances may exist and this one should not be treated as the only one.
findings.recommended_fix: Blocked on NR-062. The column's type cannot be chosen before the identity model is, since the fix is whichever of varchar or integer the catalogue's primary key ends up being. Once decided: align the type, backfill any existing values, then add the foreign-key constraint so the database enforces it.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: NOT APPLIED. Changing the column type in isolation would either break the ORM or require guessing the identity decision. Recorded so that whoever resolves NR-062 knows this reference must be constrained as part of it, rather than discovering it afterwards.
findings.verification_method: A foreign-key constraint exists on pharmacy_sale_lines.drug_catalog_id and a join to pharmacy_drug_catalog returns the expected rows.
findings.acceptance_criteria: The reference is type-compatible, constrained by the database, and joinable.
findings.regression_risk: Adding the constraint will fail if orphaned rows already exist, which is the correct outcome and must be surveyed on real data before the migration runs.

findings.title: A pharmacy sale line's drug reference is unenforced and unjoinable: varchar column against an integer primary key
findings.description: pharmacy_sale_lines.drug_catalog_id is character varying. pharmacy_drug_catalog.id is integer. The column has no foreign-key constraint — PostgreSQL cannot create one between incompatible types — so nothing prevents a sale line from recording a drug reference that matches no drug, and no join between the two tables can succeed.
